Once you see how the two relate, the rest of the documentation falls into place. If you'd rather see code first, do the Quick start and come back here. ## Overview¶ A Block is the smallest independently deployable unit. Each Block has one type and one job (an Extractor pulls records from a source, a Loader writes them to a destination) and runs as its own component with its own internal pipeline. A Blueprint is a named composition of two or more Blocks, describing a complete integration end-to-end. Recurring Blueprint shapes (Golden Record, Distribution…) are named and documented, so most new integrations start from a proven shape instead of a blank page. flowchart TD E1[Extractor

Each box is a Block, deployed as its own component; the arrows are the record flow between them, declared by the Blueprint. ## Blocks¶ A Block is an independently deployable component, versioned and scaled on its own. A Block typically consists of a processing pipeline (steps such as Deserialize, Validate, Transform, Serialize) and exchanges records with other Blocks through the wiring the Blueprint declares. Every Block has exactly one type, and each type has one narrow job. These are the Block types the framework ships today: | Block type | Job | Extractor | Pull records from a source system | Reconciler | Match and merge records that describe the same entity across sources | Assembler | Compose the canonical output shape from reconciled records | Loader | Write records to a destination system | Transactional Integration | Move records from a source system to a destination system as one atomic flow Blocks compose freely: a Blueprint can wire together any combination of Blocks the integration calls for, and no type is mandatory. A one-source, one-destination integration is just Extractor → Loader. You add a Reconciler when records about the same entity arrive from multiple sources, and an Assembler when the canonical output shape needs to be composed from those reconciled records. When the flow carries transactional data (orders, postings) rather than master data, a single Transactional Integration Block covers the whole source-to-destination flow on its own. ## Edge Blocks and core Blocks¶ Every Block type belongs to one of two groups, and the split carries the failure model. A new Block type doesn't change the model — it lands in one of these two groups. An edge Block sits at the boundary to an external system. Its job is translation: it absorbs that system's data shapes, protocols, and quirks so nothing downstream has to know the system exists (in DDD terms, an anti-corruption layer). Extractors and Loaders are edge Blocks: Extractors face systems you receive data from, Loaders face systems you deliver data to. So is a Transactional Integration, which faces both at once: even though it is an end-to-end flow from source to destination, everything it does is boundary work against systems you don't control, which is exactly what makes a Block an edge Block. Because edge Blocks deal with systems you don't control, failure there is an expected condition: the source is down, credentials expired, a record violates a business rule. Edge Blocks handle these with retries, dead-letter queues, and business incidents. A core Block owns the integration's domain model. Reconcilers and Assemblers are core Blocks: both work entirely in that model, on the integration's own representation of its entities. Any translation to or from an external system's shapes belongs to an edge Block, so a core Block only ever sees records that an edge Block has already validated and normalised. Invalid input in a core Block is therefore an integration bug, not an operational condition. That failure is a technical incident that pages someone. ## Blueprints¶ A Blueprint is a named composition of two or more Blocks: it declares which Blocks make up the integration and how records flow between them. Blueprints are versioned, reviewable, and runnable in isolation against any environment. Recurring Blueprint shapes have names. When a new requirement comes in, the first question is whether it matches one of these; if it does, you scaffold and estimate against it instead of designing from scratch. When nothing matches, you compose Blocks directly, in whatever arrangement the integration needs. The named shapes are a shortcut, not a requirement. | Blueprint | Composition | Use when | Golden Record | multiple Extractors → Reconciler → multiple Loaders | Several systems hold partial or conflicting views of the same entity, and every system should receive the merged truth (the Overview diagram) | Distribution | Extractor → multiple Loaders | One system owns the data and several others need a copy; no merging, each destination gets the records in its own shape Back to top

# Align intropy-cli terminology with the Intropy model docs

## Context

The docs page https://docs.intropy.io/concepts/intropy-model/ defines the canonical vocabulary: **Block** and **Blueprint** as the two capitalized primitives; Block types **Extractor, Reconciler, Assembler, Loader, Transactional Integration**; named Blueprint shapes **Golden Record** and **Distribution**; **records** as the thing that flows; internal pipeline steps **Deserialize, Validate, Transform, Serialize**.

A terminology audit of the CLI found the repo is mostly consistent — "integration" is itself a docs word ("a Blueprint … describ[es] a complete integration end-to-end"), and the loudest divergences (message vs record, "integration component") live in untracked scaffold output whose text originates in the **blueprints repo**, not here. The genuine CLI-repo issue: **"blueprint" is lowercase in every piece of prose** (help text, flag descriptions, README, CONTRIBUTING — ~all occurrences), while docs treat "Blueprint" as a proper-noun primitive.

Decisions made with Robin:
- **Keep `kind: Template` / `template.yaml`** — the Backstage mirroring is deliberate (`internal/blueprint/manifest.go:15-17`); treat as a known, intentional exception. No manifest changes.
- **Capitalize "Blueprint" in prose**; lowercase stays for arg placeholders, flag names, identifiers, and Go error strings.
- **Scope = this CLI repo now**, plus a follow-up checklist for cross-repo fixes.

## Changes

### 1. Capitalize "Blueprint" in user-facing prose

Rule: capitalize in cobra `Short`/`Long`/`Example` text, flag usage strings, interactive prompt text, and README/CONTRIBUTING prose. Do **not** change:
- arg placeholders / `Use` lines (`create <blueprint>`)
- Go error strings (idiomatically lowercase — `internal/blueprint/create.go:198-202` etc. stay as-is)
- code identifiers, JSON/YAML keys, paths, and the `blueprints/` directory name in the library repo (literal ref)

Files (find the full set with `grep -rn 'blueprint' cmd/ internal/ README.md CONTRIBUTING.md`, then apply the rule to prose hits only):
- `cmd/intropy/int_create.go` — `Short`, `Long` (line 31: "…from the official Intropy Blueprints library. The positional argument selects which Blueprint subdirectory…"), flag help at lines 87–88
- `cmd/intropy/int_describe.go` — `Short: "Describe an Intropy Blueprint"`, `Long` at line 23
- any other cobra commands / completion help mentioning blueprint in prose
- `internal/blueprint/` — interactive prompt/user-visible output strings only (not errors, not comments — comments may be updated where cheap but are not the goal)
- `README.md` (~14 prose occurrences), `CONTRIBUTING.md`

### 2. No other CLI text changes

Committed CLI source does not use "message", "flow", "point-to-point", or block-type names incorrectly — nothing else to fix here. Untracked dirs (`Orders/`, `Demo/`, `benchmark/`, `tmp/`) are generated/benchmark artifacts and are not edited.

## Implementation notes

- Invoke the `golang-cli` skill before editing cobra help text (house rule).
- This is a docs/UX-only change; no behavior changes, no new tests needed beyond keeping existing ones green (some tests may assert on help/prompt strings — update those assertions if they break).

## Verification

1. `go build ./... && go test ./...`
2. `go run ./cmd/intropy int create --help` and `int describe --help` — eyeball capitalized "Blueprint" in prose, lowercase `<blueprint>` placeholder intact.
3. `grep -rn 'blueprint' cmd/ internal/ README.md CONTRIBUTING.md` — remaining lowercase hits should only be identifiers, `Use:` placeholders, error strings, paths.
4. Suggest a commit point after verification (do not auto-commit).

## Follow-ups (other repos — not done in this change)

- **blueprints repo (template text that ends up in scaffolded projects):**
  - "message"/"messages" → "record(s)" in generated README/AGENTS text (docs: records flow between Blocks)
  - "integration component" → align with docs ("Block" is the deployable component; an "integration" is what a Blueprint describes)
  - Scaffolded pipeline adds a fifth `Send` step; docs list only Deserialize/Validate/Transform/Serialize as the internal steps — align docs or template wording
- **backstage-scaffold skill:** still advertises "point-to-point" — the docs page no longer uses that term (the concept is now the "Transactional Integration" Block type). Also check `golden-record`/`distribution` labels render as "Golden Record"/"Distribution" in user-facing text.
- **benchmark skill (`benchmark/skills/biztalk-migration-no-cli/SKILL.md`, untracked):** says "Blueprint = `Transactional`" — wrong term ("Transactional Integration") and wrong category (it's a Block type, not a Blueprint shape).
- **Spelling:** docs prose is British (organise/normalise), CLI text is American (-ize). Left as-is in the CLI (American is conventional for code/CLI text); raise with docs owners if a single convention is wanted.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/robinhultman/.claude/skills/golang-cli

**Persona:** You are a Go CLI engineer. You build tools that feel native to the Unix shell — composable, scriptable, and predictable under automation.

**Modes:**

- **Build** — creating a new CLI from scratch: follow the project structure, root command setup, flag binding, and version embedding sections sequentially.
- **Extend** — adding subcommands, flags, or completions to an existing CLI: read the current command tree first, then apply changes consistent with the existing structure.
- **Review** — auditing an existing CLI for correctness: check the Common Mistakes table, verify `SilenceUsage`/`SilenceErrors`, flag-to-Viper binding, exit codes, and stdout/stderr discipline.

# Go CLI Best Practices

Use Cobra + Viper as the default stack for Go CLI applications. Cobra provides the command/subcommand/flag structure and Viper handles configuration from files, environment variables, and flags with automatic layering. This combination powers kubectl, docker, gh, hugo, and most production Go CLIs.

When using Cobra or Viper, refer to the library's official documentation and code examples for current API signatures.

For trivial single-purpose tools with no subcommands and few flags, stdlib `flag` is sufficient.

## Quick Reference

| Concern             | Package / Tool                       |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| Commands & flags    | `github.com/spf13/cobra`             |
| Configuration       | `github.com/spf13/viper`             |
| Flag parsing        | `github.com/spf13/pflag` (via Cobra) |
| Colored output      | `github.com/fatih/color`             |
| Table output        | `github.com/olekukonko/tablewriter`  |
| Interactive prompts | `github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea` |
| Version injection   | `go build -ldflags`                  |
| Distribution        | `goreleaser`                         |

## Project Structure

Organize CLI commands in `cmd/myapp/` with one file per command. Keep `main.go` minimal — it only calls `Execute()`.

```
myapp/
├── cmd/
│   └── myapp/
│       ├── main.go              # package main, only calls Execute()
│       ├── root.go              # Root command + Viper init
│       ├── serve.go             # "serve" subcommand
│       ├── migrate.go           # "migrate" subcommand
│       └── version.go           # "version" subcommand
├── go.mod
└── go.sum
```

`main.go` should be minimal — see [assets/examples/main.go](assets/examples/main.go).

## Root Command Setup

The root command initializes Viper configuration and sets up global behavior via `PersistentPreRunE`. See [assets/examples/root.go](assets/examples/root.go).

Key points:

- `SilenceUsage: true` MUST be set — prevents printing the full usage text on every error
- `SilenceErrors: true` MUST be set — lets you control error output format yourself
- `PersistentPreRunE` runs before every subcommand, so config is always initialized
- Logs go to stderr, output goes to stdout

## Subcommands

Add subcommands by creating separate files in `cmd/myapp/` and registering them in `init()`. See [assets/examples/serve.go](assets/examples/serve.go) for a complete subcommand example including command groups.

## Flags

See [assets/examples/flags.go](assets/examples/flags.go) for all flag patterns:

### Persistent vs Local

- **Persistent** flags are inherited by all subcommands (e.g., `--config`)
- **Local** flags only apply to the command they're defined on (e.g., `--port`)

### Required Flags

Use `MarkFlagRequired`, `MarkFlagsMutuallyExclusive`, and `MarkFlagsOneRequired` for flag constraints.

### Flag Validation with RegisterFlagCompletionFunc

Provide completion suggestions for flag values.

### Always Bind Flags to Viper

This ensures `viper.GetInt("port")` returns the flag value, env var `MYAPP_PORT`, or config file value — whichever has highest precedence.

## Argument Validation

Cobra provides built-in validators for positional arguments. See [assets/examples/args.go](assets/examples/args.go) for both built-in and custom validation examples.

| Validator                   | Description                          |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| `cobra.NoArgs`              | Fails if any args provided           |
| `cobra.ExactArgs(n)`        | Requires exactly n args              |
| `cobra.MinimumNArgs(n)`     | Requires at least n args             |
| `cobra.MaximumNArgs(n)`     | Allows at most n args                |
| `cobra.RangeArgs(min, max)` | Requires between min and max         |
| `cobra.ExactValidArgs(n)`   | Exactly n args, must be in ValidArgs |

## Configuration with Viper

Viper resolves configuration values in this order (highest to lowest precedence):

1. **CLI flags** (explicit user input)
2. **Environment variables** (deployment config)
3. **Config file** (persistent settings)
4. **Defaults** (set in code)

See [assets/examples/config.go](assets/examples/config.go) for complete Viper integration including struct unmarshaling and config file watching.

### Example Config File (.myapp.yaml)

```yaml
port: 8080
host: localhost
log-level: info
database:
  dsn: postgres://localhost:5432/myapp
  max-conn: 25
```

With the setup above, these are all equivalent:

- Flag: `--port 9090`
- Env var: `MYAPP_PORT=9090`
- Config file: `port: 9090`

## Version and Build Info

Version SHOULD be embedded at compile time using `ldflags`. See [assets/examples/version.go](assets/examples/version.go) for the version command and build instructions.

## Exit Codes

Exit codes MUST follow Unix conventions:

| Code  | Meaning           | When to Use                               |
| ----- | ----------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| 0     | Success           | Operation completed normally              |
| 1     | General error     | Runtime failure                           |
| 2     | Usage error       | Invalid flags or arguments                |
| 64-78 | BSD sysexits      | Specific error categories                 |
| 126   | Cannot execute    | Permission denied                         |
| 127   | Command not found | Missing dependency                        |
| 128+N | Signal N          | Terminated by signal (e.g., 130 = SIGINT) |

See [assets/examples/exit_codes.go](assets/examples/exit_codes.go) for a pattern mapping errors to exit codes.

## I/O Patterns

See [assets/examples/output.go](assets/examples/output.go) for all I/O patterns:

- **stdout vs stderr**: NEVER write diagnostic output to stdout — stdout is for program output (pipeable), stderr for logs/errors/diagnostics
- **Detecting pipe vs terminal**: check `os.ModeCharDevice` on stdout
- **Machine-readable output**: support `--output` flag for table/json/plain formats
- **Colors**: use `fatih/color` which auto-disables when output is not a terminal

## Signal Handling

Signal handling MUST use `signal.NotifyContext` to propagate cancellation through context. See [assets/examples/signal.go](assets/examples/signal.go) for graceful HTTP server shutdown.

## Shell Completions

Cobra generates completions for bash, zsh, fish, and PowerShell automatically. See [assets/examples/completion.go](assets/examples/completion.go) for both the completion command and custom flag/argument completions.

## Testing CLI Commands

Test commands by executing them programmatically and capturing output. See [assets/examples/cli_test.go](assets/examples/cli_test.go).

Use `cmd.OutOrStdout()` and `cmd.ErrOrStderr()` in commands (instead of `os.Stdout` / `os.Stderr`) so output can be captured in tests.

## Common Mistakes

| Mistake | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| Writing to `os.Stdout` directly | Tests can't capture output. Use `cmd.OutOrStdout()` which tests can redirect to a buffer |
| Calling `os.Exit()` inside `RunE` | Cobra's error handling, deferred functions, and cleanup code never run. Return an error, let `main()` decide |

1	# intropy CLI

3	`intropy` is the command-line interface for working with Intropy integrations
4	and agent skills. It does two things:

1	# Backstage Scaffolder Module: intropy
2	
3	A [Backstage](https://backstage.io) scaffolder backend module that provides the
4	`intropy:int:create` action for scaffolding integrations from
5	[intropy](https://github.com/integrio-intropy) blueprints.
6	
7	The action shells out to the `intropy` CLI inside the scaffolder workspace, so the
8	CLI remains the single source of scaffolding logic. The module adapts it to the
9	Backstage scaffolder: workspace-relative paths, structured errors, and registered
10	outputs.
11	
12	## Installation
13	
14	Add the package to your Backstage backend:
15	
16	```bash
17	yarn --cwd packages/backend add @intropy/backstage-plugin-scaffolder-backend-module-intropy
18	```
19	
20	Register the module in `packages/backend/src/index.ts`:
21	
22	```ts
23	backend.add(
24	  import('@intropy/backstage-plugin-scaffolder-backend-module-intropy'),
25	);
26	```
27	
28	## Runtime requirement: the intropy CLI
29	
30	The action runs the `intropy` binary, so it must be available in the environment
31	where the scaffolder backend runs. In a container image, copy it from the CLI
32	image:
33	
34	```dockerfile
35	ARG INTROPY_CLI_VERSION=v0.5.0
36	FROM ghcr.io/integrio-intropy/intropy-cli:${INTROPY_CLI_VERSION} AS intropy-cli
37	
38	# ... in the runtime stage:
39	COPY --from=intropy-cli /usr/local/bin/intropy /usr/local/bin/intropy
40	```
41	
42	By default the action invokes `intropy` from `PATH`. To point at a specific
43	binary (useful for local development), set the optional app-config:
44	
45	```yaml
46	intropy:
47	  cli:
48	    path: /path/to/intropy
49	```
50	
51	## Usage in a template
52
